2. Pre-exercise food helps settle the stomach, absorbs some of the gastric juices
and abates hunger feelings.
The caloric density of a snack or meal affects the rate at which the food leaves
your stomach. This explains why you can exercise comfortably soon after
snacking on a few crackers or a
piece of fruit, but you are better
off waiting three or four hours
after eating a heartier meal. The
general pre-exercise “rule of
thumb” is to allow:
•
3–4 hours for a large meal to
digest
•
2–3 hours for a smaller meal
•
1–2 hours for a blended or
liquid meal
•
less than an hour for a small
snack, as tolerated
3. Pre-exercise food fuels the
muscles. The snack you eat even
an hour before you run gets
digested into glucose and burned
for energy. For example, one
study showed that runners who
ate 400 calories of sugar three
hours before an easy four-hour
run burned about 70 percent of
